title: Wisconsin’s municipalities feeling the pinch of high fuel costs - WPR
text: Every month, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway can see some of what the United States’ war with Iran is costing her constituents.  The cost to fuel both the city’s diesel and gasoline vehicles has increased by $222,580 a month since last year — a spike she attributes in part to the fighting with Iran and subsequent shipping disruptions. That monthly increase doesn’t include the city’s bus system. “It is serious and the impact of this unnecessary war and inflation is really impacting our budget,” Rhodes-Conway told “ Wisconsin Today .” “If we don’t see some relief on this soon, we’re going to be spending millions more for fuel this year, and that money has to come from somewhere, right? So that’s a direct impact to our taxpayers, to the essential services that we provide.” WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Fuel costs are pinching municipal budgets around the state, and some of them could be forced to dip into their reserves to cover the added cost and make agonizing decisions for next year’s budgets, which are now being drafted. The city of Kaukauna — a city of about 18,000 people near Appleton — has seen fuel costs roughly double from last year, said Mayor Tony Penterman. So far, Kaukauna is under budget for the year. But with fall leaf pickup and winter snow plowing yet to come, which typically rack up a lot of miles for its diesel trucks, he is worried that the city won’t stay in the black.  “If we have a couple ice storms or snowstorms, at that $6.01 a gallon, that could put us over budget real fast in 2026 leading into 2027, which will be even more stressful,” Penterman said. The extra cost for fuel is putting pressure on other government functions. It drives up inflation, making street reconstruction or amenities like park pavilions more expensive. The city is due to upgrade its cybersecurity and is looking at hiring for new positions. Officials will have to make some tough decisions. “It’s hard to manage a city our size when you try to keep the tax rate under control,” Penterman said. Stevens Point Mayor Mike Wiza said his city is also feeling the pinch and has been looking for ways to conserve fuel. One has been to reduce idling time of city vehicles. “I don’t know how much it saves, but it’s something,” Wiza said. “If the vehicle is off for 15 minutes, you’re saving money.”  Figures provided by the city of Madison illustrate just how much monthly fuel bills can add up, especially for larger cities. Last September, the city paid $3.20 for a gallon of diesel. This September, the cost had climbed to $6.25 — an increase of $3.05 per gallon. The city was paying $2.90 a gallon for regular gasoline last September; that price jumped to $4.62.  Madison uses 50,000 gallons of diesel a month on average for its large fleet vehicles, which include fire trucks, garbage trucks and other public works vehicles. The Madison Metro bus system uses another 67,000 gallons of diesel a month. Madison’s gasoline fleet consumes, on average, 34,000 gallons a month.  The city doesn’t have many options for reducing fuel consumption. Police and fire trucks have to respond to calls, garbage has to be picked up, the buses need to run. “There’s some basic services that you just have to keep doing, and they have to use the fuel that they use,” Rhodes-Conway said. The city has traditionally bought some fuel with a contract that locks in a price. “Now, we don’t want to lock in a contract right now at this price because there’s a chance that it goes down and then we lose,” she said.  But the higher fuel costs underscore for the mayor the wisdom of the city’s efforts to invest in electric and hybrid vehicles.  “It doesn’t save us on diesel, but it does save us on gasoline because for every EV that we drive for 5,000 miles, that’s over 400 gallons of fuel that we’re saving that we don’t have to pay for,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Just saving on the fuel cost alone means that it makes sense for us to invest in these types of vehicles, so that we don’t have to deal with this volatility in the price of fossil fuels.”

title: Madison's police monitor is unique in Wisconsin. But the office has been dogged by controversies - WPR
text: In 2020, Madison’s Common Council voted to create the city’s first-ever independent police monitor. That vote, which followed years of advocacy, came toward the end of a public meeting that spanned nearly nine hours . During hours of public comment, most residents spoke in favor. The Office of Madison’s Independent Police Monitor intended to provide a civilian-led check on the Madison Police Department, and the powers of the position are unique in Wisconsin. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. But since its inception, the office has weathered controversy after controversy. Those disputes have involved heated public meetings, human resources investigations and a restraining order. The office — and the controversies surrounding it — are receiving heightened attention after a fatal police shooting on July 22. A total of four Madison cops are on leave after one of those officers, Kiel Baitinger-Peterson , shot Corey Ruiz , a 38-year-old Black resident. It will be up to Dane County’s district attorney to decide whether to charge the officers involved in that shooting, following a criminal investigation from Wisconsin’s Department of Justice. At the same time, the city’s interim police monitor, Aeiramique Glass, has launched her own investigation into the shooting . In protests that arose after the city moved to clear an encampment at the site of the shooting , Glass was involved in a physical altercation with police. In a video posted online, she said she would “f—ing burn this city to the ground.” The comments drew condemnation from the city’s mayor. But Glass doesn’t work for the mayor, and the mayor has no power to discipline or remove her. After the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020, the number of communities adopting civilian oversight of police went up “fairly exponentially,” said Cameron McEllhiney, the executive director of the National Association for Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement, or NACOLE. She says those efforts help bolster trust and improve transparency. “In the United States, we have a very polarized relationship between community and police,” McEllhiney said. “It’s a way for police to better understand the communities that they are serving (and) it’s a way for community to better understand police practices.” Nationwide, roughly 250 communities have some type of a police oversight agency, according to NACOLE. Many of those entities operate in large or mid-sized cities, but they vary widely in their powers and structure. In Wisconsin, the city’s police monitor and the civilian-led board that oversees it, are one-of-a-kind. “No other Wisconsin municipality has enacted ordinances establishing an agency or body charged with civilian oversight of its police department,” Madison’s city attorney wrote in a legal memo this summer. Under the ordinance that Madison adopted in 2020, the police monitor has the power to investigate complaints made by members of the public against Madison officers and the Madison Police Department. The monitor’s office can release conclusions from those reports, and it can make recommendations. Ultimately, however, the Office of the Independent Police Monitor, or OIPM, lacks the authority to discipline cops. That authority lies with the Police and Fire Commission , a separate city board that predates the monitor. Across the country, there are other cities where police monitors can review complaints and monitor critical policing incidents. In many communities, that monitor reports to the city council, the mayor or another executive, like a city manager. Madison’s situation, where the monitor is under the authority of a civilian oversight board, is less common but not unprecedented, McEllhiney said. When Madison adopted its ordinance, supporters argued that structure would help insulate the monitor from political pressure. They also wanted to make sure there was a seat at the table for community members, including those who might typically be left out of city politics. “When you have a person who’s been appointed by the mayor, there’s always the risk that the mayor will appoint someone who will only make decisions that they like,” said Sharon Fairley , a University of Chicago law professor, who previously worked as the chief administrator of Chicago’s Independent Police Review Authority. “Each structure has its pros and cons.” Madison’s structure has meant that — even as the mayor and some city council member express frustrations with the current police monitor — those elected officials have limited control over the situation. Madison’s ordinance says that the monitor reports directly to the executive subcommittee of the Police Civilian Oversight Board, or PCOB. The PCOB is responsible for nominating police monitors with the Common Council’s approval. PCOB Chair Maia Pearson did not respond to emailed questions from WPR. But based on public meetings and past statements, PCOB leadership appears to be standing behind the city’s current police monitor. More than a decade ago, Madison was reeling from another police shooting, after city officer Matt Kenny killed 19-year-old Tony Robinson in March 2015. That led to the creation of an ad hoc committee. That committee’s very first recommendation was to create an independent police monitor. The city’s Police Civilian Oversight Board met for the first time in November 2020. In late 2022, the PCOB hired attorney Robin Copley as the city’s first independent police monitor. That decision came after at least two other previously picked candidates backed out of consideration . After Copley started work, it took nearly two years for the monitor’s office to set up a form, so it could begin taking complaints. The office didn’t release its first annual report until 2025, and some council members raised concerns about Copley’s management and lack of response to public records requests . In October 2025, Copley resigned, citing medical reasons. Shortly before, the PCOB had convened a closed-session meeting to discuss her job performance. In fall 2025, the PCOB chose Aeiramique Glass as Madison’s interim police monitor. That job description said she was expected to serve for six to nine months, and that she would act as a hiring manager in the search for a permanent police monitor. In June, the Common Council voted unanimously to extend Glass’ contract through March 2027 , or until a permanent police monitor is hired. If that contract were to be terminated early, that decision would likely have to come from a Common Council vote, City Attorney Mike Haas told WPR. Glass previously served as Baltimore’s acting chief of police accountability. She filed a whistleblower lawsuit against Baltimore in 2025, alleging that she was terminated from that role in a discriminatory and retaliatory manner . Glass’ current annual salary is $147,741. When she took office in Madison, Glass said she encountered a backlog of 18 complaints against police, and she says she’s been steadily working through those. By spring 2026, eight complaints had been closed, according to an annual OIPM report which is dated to March 26 . The office has a staff of three people — Glass, a full-time office manager and part-time analyst Greg Gelembiuk. For 2026, the OIPM’s total operating budget was approved at $405,000. “The office is finally doing what it was created to do, and doing it without the resources necessary, without the staffing necessary,” Glass said in an interview with WPR this week. This spring, Glass released and then retracted her first annual report as monitor. The report included a cover image generated by artificial intelligence that hallucinated Madison’s skyline with two state Capitol buildings . Police Chief John Patterson also said that a section of the report included incorrect information about citations against juveniles. Glass said she used AI on a limited basis to create elements of the report and its cover image. She apologized, and later issued a revised version. “I really, truly take accountability for the ignorance of not really and truly understanding how much the skyline means to this community,” Glass said during a news conference. Despite missteps, Glass and her supporters also point to successes. Some of the office’s conclusions have been major. Earlier this year, the office released a report that disputed the official cause of death for 32-year-old Richard Lee Johnson. Dane County’s medical examiner previously concluded that Johnson died “accidentally due to complications from cocaine toxicity.” The OIPM, however, hired its own forensic pathologist, Dr. Victor Weedn, who concluded that, while cocaine may have contributed to Johnson’s death, the actual cause was cardiac arrest because of the way Johnson was restrained by police. After completing the OIPM report, Weedn was later hired by Dane County as a deputy medical examiner. As a result of that report, the OIPM and other city leaders urged the Dane County medical examiner’s office to reopen its investigation into Johnson’s cause and manner of death. It’s not clear whether the medical examiner has done so — the office’s director of operations Cristina Figueroa Soto did not respond to an inquiry from WPR. Meanwhile, top city officials including the city attorney, finance director and human resources director have been raising alarms about the monitor’s conduct. In an Aug. 31 memo to the Common Council president, those officials wrote that the OIPM was flouting multiple city procedures, including failing to meet budget deadlines and failing to follow rules for contracting and purchasing. The memo also alleged an OIPM staffer had been working remotely from another country without a valid telework agreement in place. In response, Glass has asserted that the OIPM does not have to follow city Administrative Procedure Memoranda, or APMs. “As you know, we do not have to comply with APMs other than what we do in good faith when I feel comfortable doing so,” Glass wrote to the city attorney on July 31. “I have never given you independent contractors’ information, and I will not start with this case.” According to the memo, the city has hired an external firm to investigate multiple human resources complaints involving OIPM staff. Meanwhile, Glass is embroiled in a dispute over access to MPD records from the shooting of Ruiz. Glass says Madison’s ordinance grants her unfettered access to those records. The city attorney argues that state law prevents police from releasing them while an investigation by the district attorney is still ongoing. That prompted Glass to file a lawsuit on Aug. 20, asking a judge to order the records’ release. Earlier in August, police released drone footage showing the altercation between Glass and police near where people were protesting. OIPM’s data analyst posted, then a deleted a video to Facebook, in which Glass talks to the camera just after the scuffle happened. In the video , Glass holds up her hand, which is bleeding. “They’ve been wanting to do this to me,” Glass says in the video. “I will f—ing burn this city down.” Glass has said she was speaking figuratively. “’I will burn this city down’ has been used throughout history as a metaphor for dismantling corruption, exposing injustice and demanding accountability,” the OIPM’s attorney William Sulton said at the time. PCOB leaders also defended Glass, saying the focus should be on the conduct of police. But Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway took a sharper tone. “I think it’s disturbing anytime a city employee is calling for violence,” Rhodes-Conway said at a news conference. In September, a Dane County judge granted a four-year restraining order to a Madison police officer who was involved with that incident. It orders Glass to stay away from that officer. In court documents, the officer wrote that Glass had grabbed her arm and pushed her. Some council members including Carmella Glenn and Julia Matthews have been staunch defenders of Monitor Glass. “Everybody hated her because she challenged the system,” Glenn said of some officials’ attitudes toward Glass. Other alders have emphasized that the role of the police monitor is vital, but say the office is failing to live up to its promise. “The operational conflicts and some of the divisiveness that has come from the office has gotten in the way of actually just doing that work,” Council President Sabrina Madison said. As an example, Madison pointed to a lengthy Facebook Live session , in which Glenn and Glass criticized multiple city employees by name. “I don’t want a monitor who’s going to sit on Facebook for two hours and drag a department agency and other alders, other community members,” Madison said. “I just don’t want that because that gets away from what the ordinance talks about (which is) building relationships.” Madison says she plans to use money from the Common Council’s budget to hire a mediator, so that she can meet with PCOB Chair Pearson and work through conflicts. This month, alders voted down a request to increase the OIPM’s budget by $28,500. And, during that discussion, many alders voiced concerns about OIPM operations. Among them was Alder Joann Pritchett, who alluded to Glass’ run-in with police in early August. “The monitor became the story when she inserted herself at the encampment site — that’s a no-no,” Pritchett said. “I have looked at my dictionary meaning of monitor, and it does not mean inserting yourself. It means standing back, making observations, making contemporaneous notes so that you know what happenened.” Glass told WPR she attends protests, so she can monitor what’s going on as part of her duties. Additionally, Madison’s OIPM ordinance specifies that the monitor should conduct “community outreach.” “I’m not really sure what they would perceive as participation in protest,” Glass said of her critics. “When I’m asked to be in community, that is a part of my job.” Fairley, a law professor who has studied civilian oversight, says it’s crucial that an independent monitor not be seen as overly for or against the local police. “Civilian oversight is supposed to be neutral,” Fairley said. “If you have a monitor that’s going out and protesting against the police, then the rank-and-file police officers are not going to think that they’re going to get a fair shot.” In an interview with WPR, Alder Will Ochowicz said he’s not necessarily opposed to the monitor attending protests. Rather, he says he concerns center around Glass’ management and job performance. “I want independent police oversight,” Ochowicz said at a September Common Council meeting. “But every single step of this has been adversarial between I.M. Glass and the city.” Just before his term expired this spring, former Alder MGR Govindarajan introduced an amendment , intended to beef up the OIPM’s reporting requirements and to clarify that the police monitor must follow city administrative procedures. Alders Yannette Figueroa Cole, Derek Field, Ochowicz and Madison signed on to that proposal. But, in the immediate aftermath of Ruiz’s death, all the sponsors agreed to withdraw their amendments. “At a moment when our community is grieving and looking to its leaders to strengthen trust in our systems of accountability, I believe it is important that we create space for collaboration rather than continue a process that many believe has become increasingly divisive,” Madison wrote in a blog post this July. The legislation could be reintroduced, although Madison and Ochowicz say they have no immediate plans to do so. There’s also the question of what the OIPM’s next budget will look like. Citing a shortfall, Rhodes-Conway instructed all department heads to submit proposals that cut their spending by at least 2 percent. The OIPM’s budget request, however, asks for that office’s operating budget to be increased to $781,158 in 2027. Additionally, Glass asked for $1.63 million in “emergency funding” for the OIPM, pointing to allocated OIPM funding that reverted to the city’s general fund after going unspent from 2000 to 2025. Going forward, Glass has also urged city officials to set a funding floor for the OIPM at 1 percent of the MPD budget. The department’s 2026 operating budget is more than $98 million . Glass did not submit a budget narrative form or formal transmittal memo by the city’s deadline for department heads of July 17. Instead, she sent a letter on July 27, explaining why she did not follow that process. “This letter is formal notice that the Office of the Independent Police Monitor needs immediate action, not the routine budget process,” Glass wrote . “I was in the process of preparing the narrative and explanation forms that accompany that submission when this community experienced the killing of a Black man by police, and my attention turned to this office’s rapid response and to the community in the aftermath. What I submitted in Munis was an attempt to participate in a budget process that is not, in its current form, an equitable one.” Ruiz was shot on July 22, five days after the deadline for agency budget requests. Rhodes-Conway will submit her operating budget proposal next week. And ultimately, the Common Council will vote on how much money the police monitor’s office should get. title: Signal chat for alders is legal, but still raises questions - Madison365
text: A group chat among Madison alders using the secure messaging app Signal is legal, as long as no Common Council business is discussed, City Attorney Mike Haas said. But a freedom of information advocate said it still raises questions because the app’s disappearing messages function makes it impossible to know whether Alders used it to discuss proposals before the council. One Signal group chat brought to Madison365’s attention has been active since April 2025, started by former alder MGR Govindaranjan following that spring election. It currently has eight members, but has previously had as many as 12. Various members have set the “disappearing messages” function to automatically delete messages at varying intervals from eight hours to one week, according to screen shots obtained by Madison365. Why Signal raises questions Signal is regarded as one of the most secure messaging apps, as it employs end-to-end encryption and does not store messages or user data on a central server. That means once messages are received and deleted, they’re gone forever and can’t be retrieved or released, even under a court order. That raises an open records question for Bill Lueders, president of the Wisconsin Freedom of Information Council. “My question is, why are they using Signal Chat?” Lueders said. “It seems to me the only distinction or advantage is that it allows them to communicate secretly without people being able to have a record of their communication, which to me sounds like they’re trying to break the law.” The use of any messaging app – even email – also raises questions regarding open meetings law, which prohibits discussion of official business among a quorum of members (in Madison, that means 14) without public notice. In fact, the City of Madison posts public notices of social functions where 14 or more Alders might be in attendance. In his onboarding presentation for new alders , Haas notes that it’s also prohibited to gather enough members to potentially form a negative quorum – that is, enough potential votes to block any proposal. In some cases, that could be as few as five; 12 would always constitute a negative quorum. In 2020, then-City Attorney Michael May wrote in a formal opinion that any meeting of five or more alders should be given public notice. But neither open records law nor the open meetings law, nor the relevant city of Madison ordinances, would be applicable to purely personal conversations.  Every Alder who responded to questions from Madison365 said the Signal group chat in question was only used for personal communications. Some said Signal was used in other instances for communication regarding City business, but that they saved such messages to comply with open records law. Council Friends 2025 Screen shots provided to Madison365 indicate that Govindaranjan started the group, called “Council Friends 2025,” on April 15, 2025, two weeks after the April 1 spring election and the day the new council was sworn in. Messages were initially set to disappear after eight hours; District 1 Alder John Duncan, who has since left the council and the chat group, disabled disappearing messages. “Good idea to have disappearing messages off, I think,” Govindarajan wrote in the group. “Main reminder for this group: no city business can be discussed here.” He then announced that the group would have a “friends hangout/election-celebration” at the Paradise bar in Madison the following Saturday. According to the screenshots, then-newly-elected alder Carmella Glenn, who is now vice president of the Council, reactivated the disappearing messages function and set it to delete messages after eight hours on April 21.  Glenn told Madison365 that she didn’t recall activating that setting. “I apologize. I was not thinking about open records,” she said. “I didn’t even know enough about open records. It was my first day.” No screenshots reviewed by Madison365 indicate that anyone disabled the disappearing messages function in the nearly 18 months since. In fact, several members adjusted the timing of automatic message deletion. Screen shots indicate that Govindarajan left the group after the spring 2026 election, in which he did not run for re-election, and Duncan left the group in July, when he resigned his seat because he was moving out of the city. Govindaranjan made District 10 Alder Yanette Figueroa Cole the group’s administrator. Both she and Council President Sabrina Madison left the group on July 24, two days after Madison police shot and killed Corey Ruiz. Neither answered a question from Madison365 asking why they left the group. Figueroa Cole made Alder Julia Matthews administrator of the group when she left. As of September 28, eight members remained in the group: Glenn, Matthews, and Alders Derek Fields, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, John Guequirre, Regina Vidaver, Sean O’Brien and Will Ochowicz.  Madison365 sent a number of questions to all the current members of the group; those who responded said they only used the group for personal purposes such as scheduling social gatherings and sharing news or announcements.  “I use Signal as an easy way to share news and for social planning in a more secure platform than texting,” Vidaver wrote in an email to Madison365. “I do not remember any Council business being conducted in the Signal group.” “The chat referenced (in Madison365’s questions) was not used for the purpose of conducting official communications and therefore does not fall within the retention requirement outlined in” Madison ordinances, Figueroa Cole wrote. “The chat was created originally as a post-election for current and newly elected alders who had met before the election,” Ochowicz wrote. “No city business was discussed in the chat, it was mainly to notify of events like parties or barbeques, or to share notifications from Voces De Fronteras on ICE sightings.” “Shortly after I joined the Council in January 2024, one or more alders shared that the Signal app had been used for some time for non-city business, that is, social interactions,” Guequirre wrote. “I had not used the app previously, but saw no objection to the platform for the described purpose … Typical chats have involved (1) where to meet socially, (2) event recommendations, (3) reading recommendations, (4) other social interactions. Two of the longest chats I can remember involved vacation photos and recipes … I hesitate to say Council and Committee business has never been discussed because it takes a little time to absorb all of the nuances of the open meetings and open records laws. When business ends up in a post, veteran alders are quick to ‘coach’ the novices.” No alders who responded to Madison365 acknowledged being members of other Signal groups; screenshots from a different group administered by Martinez-Rutherford indicate she shut it down after receiving questions from Madison365. That group had 11 members, four of whom are no longer members of the council, and a former alder who was a member said the group was not active and she wasn’t even aware the group existed until she got a notification that the group had been closed. Guequirre and Glenn both gave examples of council business being discussed via Signal outside the group chat.  Guequirre said he received a Signal message from Vidaver about cosponsorship of a resolution; knowing that constituted City business, he saved the message, he said. Glenn provided screen shots to Madison365 showing messages from Figueroa Cole containing background information on funding for a men’s homeless shelter. Figueroa Cole had the messages set to delete after one day; Glenn took a screen shot for records retention purposes. Glenn said after receiving an open records request in August, she started to realize the potential problems of using Signal, especially among so many members. “I want it to stop,” she said. What the law says Madison General Ordinance says city officials, which includes city employees as well as elected alders, “shall refrain” from communicating via text message or instant messaging “for official communications purposes or for matters that would result in a public record if another format such as email or written communications were employed, unless the employee or official preserves a copy of such communications.” Haas said that means personal communications via text or instant message are allowed, as personal communications do not constitute public records, and that it’s also permissible to discuss official business if those messages are saved. The same is true on the open meetings question: it’s permissible for more than five alders to gather or have a conversation, as long as they don’t discuss city business. But due to the nature of Signal, the media and the community are left to take officials at their word that they’re not using it to discuss city business. Other forms of communication are generally preserved, and even if alders exclude communications they deem as personal from open records requests, a court could adjudicate otherwise and compel such records be released. “Rightly or wrongly, the state’s open meetings law seeks to ensure that the deliberative process plays out in public, that people aren’t going around cutting backdoor deals and reaching decisions outside of the public forum where they meet as a body,” said Lueders of the Freedom of Information Council. “They’re supposed to hash out their government business in a public setting. Those deliberations are supposed to be taking place in a public venue and not behind closed doors and not behind closed apps.”

title: Madison officials say city is ready to manage clerk’s maternity leave during election - Wisconsin Examiner
text: Madison officials say the city is prepared to manage Clerk Lydia McComas' maternity leave during the Nov. 3 election, even with the added scrutiny that comes with recent high-profile errors. title: Office of Independent Police Monitor sees no change from 2026 in 2027 budget - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis. -- On Tuesday, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway released her 2027 executive operational budget. Save for the cost of living adjustment, the Office of the Independent Police Monitor's budget remained the same from the previous year in the mayor's proposal. "As you know, that was the only agency that didn't submit any 2% reduction and didn't meet our budget deadlines or follow the process at all," Mayor Rhodes-Conway said. "So we just gave them a flat cost-to-continue budget." In her 2027 request , which was submitted late, Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass requested $781,931. The mayor's proposed budget for the office in 2027 is $432,328. "I did not submit a reduction proposal alongside that request," Monitor Glass said in her letter to the mayor, dated July 27. "This office was created to provide independent civilian oversight of a police department with an approx. $98 million dollar budget, and this office currently operates on less than one half of on percent of that figure." Along with her request, Glass asked for "$1.63 million in unspent OIPM budget authority from 2020 through 2025 to be restored to this office as emergency funding." Additionally, Glass asked for an annual floor of a minimum of 1% of the Madison Police Department's budget. The mayor's proposal would give $107 million to that department next year. In the letter, Glass said she was in the process of preparing the forms to accompany her submission, but the deadly officer-involved shooting of Corey Ruiz, which happened on July 22 , turned her attention to rapid response and the community. Budget submissions to the mayor's office were due on July 17. Glass said in her letter that her office has been underfunded and understaffed. Currently, there are only three people working in the OIPM, including Glass. One of those staff members, the data analyst, isn't even full time. Glass' request, which was shot down, was to make that staffer a full-time data and forensics manager. Ronal Serpas, a professor at Loyola University in New Orleans, has led several major law enforcement agencies and served as the superintendent of the New Orleans Police Dept. His past work included working alongside police monitors. "A full-time person to do data analytics probably makes a lot of sense to a lot of people, including me, because it really is analyzing what's already happened," Serpas said. According to the National Association for Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement , oversight bodies like Glass' office should have enough money to fulfill their duties. Also on Tuesday, the Police Civilian Oversight Board released a statement. That statement said the OIPM needed adequate funding in order to ensure the office is fully-staffed and equipped to fulfill the responsibilities the city has assigned to it. The board also said that only it can provide an official employment review of Glass, and that any other review should not be treated as official. Last week, News 3 Now obtained a 42-page employment review of Glass from the City Attorney's office. The budget hasn't been adopted yet. title: Madison’s funding proposal could support men’s shelter 24/7 operations - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway wants to put an extra $1 million toward ensuring the city’s new men’s shelter can stay open around the clock — a goal shelter leaders have pushed for since before the building even opened. Rhodes-Conway introduced her 2027 operating budget proposal on Tuesday. The city’s Finance Committee takes it up later this month, with a final Common Council vote set for November. Right now, the shelter, located on Bartillion Drive , is only open overnight. The mayor’s proposal would keep the $1.7 million in shelter operations funding the city already provides alongside Dane County. It would also add $1 million toward an endowment through Shelter Friends of Dane County, a nonprofit that started the endowment to help cover operating costs with support from the community. Combined, that would complete the city’s $2 million pledge toward round-the-clock operations. “But you’re right, it’s one thing to build a building, and it’s another thing to have the funds to operate it,” Rhodes-Conway said. Karla Thennes, executive director of Porchlight, said the mayor understands the importance of the shelter operating 24/7. “I think the mayor really understands the importance of the shelter being open 24/7, right? Like that’s where I say that’s where the magic happens, right?” Thennes said. Thennes said overnight hours mostly cover the basics — meals, showers, case management, sleep. The daytime hours are where the real work happens. “At nighttime, people are eating, they’re showering, they’re meeting with the case manager, they’re going to bed, right? There’s just not a lot you can do. But during the day is when they’re getting connected to the resources, when they’re getting connected to jobs and moving into housing,” Thennes said. Porchlight has already lined up about a year’s worth of funding to get daytime hours up and running, Thennes said. She added that the mayor’s commitment to the endowment has both Porchlight and Shelter Friends “thrilled.” “We’ve got to get that daytime program going to really help folks. This isn’t permanent housing. This is shelter. We need people to move up and out. And so that would be the next step,” Thennes said. Kristin Rucinski, executive director for Shelter Friends of Dane County, Inc., wrote in a statement to WMTV: “We are very grateful to Mayor Rhodes-Conway, the Common Council and City staff for continuing to make homelessness a priority. We really see the proposed $1M endowment contribution as a critical piece of the City’s overall commitment. And we hope their commitment does exactly what the mayor said and rallies additional community investment for 24/7 operations to help more men move from homelessness to housing.” Thennes said the number of people coming to shelters has kept climbing since the COVID-19 pandemic. “The cost of affordable housing has become unaffordable, right? So it’s difficult for people to live in the community. Those of us who do have affordable housing, Porchlight has 350 units of affordable housing. We have long waiting lists,” Thennes said. “20% of our shelter guests are employed; they’re out there, they’re working their shifts, they’re coming back, they’re reserving a bed. title: Wisconsin officials rehash Act 10, heads to state Supreme Court for first time in over a decade - The Daily Cardinal
text: Demonstrators gathered in the Capitol to protest the controversial Act 10 legislation in spring of 2011, which limited state workers’ rights to collective bargaining. The legislation is currently being challenged in court. Democratic officials across Wisconsin argue Act 10 is harming workers across the state, pushing for repeals amid the 2026 midterm elections. Former GOP Gov. Scott Walker enacted Act 10 in 2011 and has been a contentious topic between Republican and Democratic state officials since it was put into law. Democrats have attempted to repeal the law multiple times, but have not succeeded.  The law curtailed collective bargaining rights for most public sector employees, limiting negotiations to base wage increases capped at the consumer price index. There have been claims against Act 10, saying it has harmed teacher retention. State Sen. Kelda Roys told The Daily Cardinal Wisconsin is facing a teacher retention crisis because of  Act 10. “It's harder for young people to make the decision to go into teaching because they know they're likely to not be able to afford to buy a house, have children or live in the communities where they're teaching because their wages have not kept up with inflation,” Roys said. “The benefits that were once the big draw of public sector employment are being ratcheted down, and the employees are bearing a greater share of those costs.” Madison Teachers Inc. told the Cardinal Act 10 has left Madison schools “starved” for funds. Dr. Joe Gothard, superintendent of Madison Metropolitan School District (MMSD), told the Cardinal MMSD has had to rely on outside reinforcements for its budget. “Our community has supported referendums to make sure we have the operational capacity to afford our employees’ wage increases,” Gothard said. “That's been critical.” Lawmakers in favor of Act 10 argue union stipulations allow for greater district flexibility. The Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty (WILL) actively defends Act 10’s merits and represents teachers in support of the law. Will Flanders, the research director for WILL, said the act has allowed school districts to save over $1.6 billion annually by shifting district costs onto employees. “School districts have been given a lot more freedom in terms of their hiring practices and how they reward teachers for good performance,” Flanders told the Cardinal. “They can be more creative in their pay systems.” Roys disagreed, calling the argument “dubious.” “There is literally not one community in the state that has adequate funding to meet the needs of their residents and provide basic public services,” Roys said. She notes most districts, like MMSD , have to utilize referendums to support funding. In November, more than 70 districts will have referendums on the ballot . This past April, 60% of the 75 referendums in the spring election passed. Roys also said Act 10 is hurting Wisconsin’s performance as a whole against neighboring states like Minnesota. “[It’s] very challenging for our state to compete economically,” Roys said. “If you look at our performance versus Minnesota's — the economic performance, the educational attainment and salaries — we've just fallen behind our peer states. I think debasing workers' rights is one of the reasons why.” Other officials echoed Roys, such as Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who told the Cardinal Act 10 blocked local governments from providing basic services. “Act 10 did not give local governments like Madison more budget flexibility because it was tied to a dramatic cut in shared revenue from the state,” Rhodes-Conway told the Cardinal. “My hope for the next state administration is that union rights are restored.” Gubernatorial candidates Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Democrat Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley have competing points of view on the topic as well. Crowley told the Cardinal he would work to repeal Act 10 if elected.  “As governor, I’ll work to repeal Act 10 to make sure Wisconsinites get the fair wages and benefits they deserve,” Crowley said in an email statement to the Cardinal. “What I won’t do is support extreme policies that raise costs on everyday families like MAGA Congressman Tom Tiffany, who called union workers ‘ kingpins ’ and has spent his entire career selling out working Wisconsinites .” Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who was elected in 2018, has opposed the law, attempting to repeal parts of the act through budget proposals, but nothing has stuck in the courts. Tiffany emphasized the damage he believes a repeal of Act 10 would cost citizens. “Talk to local governments and school districts across Wisconsin, and they will tell you that repealing Act 10 would saddle them with enormous new costs,” Tiffany said in an email statement to the Cardinal. “They would be forced to make devastating cuts or come back to taxpayers for more money. Repealing Act 10 would cost taxpayers roughly $2 billion more every year.” Aside from impacts on educators, Democratic state Sen. Chris Larson said corrections workers suffer the most. There is currently a 33% vacancy rate in correction officer positions across the state. “It’s thankless, stressful work that negatively impacts the health and life expectancy of those doing it,” Larson said in a statement to the Cardinal. “Worker shortages cause forced overtime, which causes burnout, which exacerbates worker shortages. As a result, the Wisconsin Department of Corrections and Wisconsin Counties have had to drastically increase the pay of Corrections Officers – and still they struggle to recruit good candidates, who often value work-life balance more than financial compensation.” In a 2024 survey , over half of the Wisconsin correction officers surveyed said if they left their position, it would be due to their salary and benefits. Larson said if Act 10 were repealed it would make a “huge difference” for Wisconsin correction workers. The debate over Act 10 is highly partisan, with many Democratic officials speaking out about its damage to public sector employees and Republican officials arguing the financial benefits the law brings. If the law heads to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, there is a chance for repeal under the 5-2 liberal majority, according to Flanders. Federal courts upheld the law in Wisconsin Education Association Council (WEAC) v. Walker in 2013, and lawmakers have deferred to the precedent. The case focused on the legality of the differentiation between general and public safety workers.  WEAC and the American Federation of State, County & Municipal Employees (AFSCME) filed a lawsuit against the 2011 law in 2023, arguing the state’s Equal Protection Clause made the law unconstitutional. Flanders said WEAC and AFSCME’s case is a “legitimate threat” to Act 10. Dane County Circuit Court Judge Jacob Frost struck down over 60 sections of Act 10 in late 2024, but stayed his decision for a state ruling. In July 2026, however, the Wisconsin Court of Appeals District 2 overturned Frost’s ruling, relegalizing the full scope of Act 10. Now labor groups have appealed the case to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, which will review the decision for the first time since 2014 if the petition is accepted. Jane Dardik is the City News Editor. She has covered a wide array of Madison stories, including city elections, budgets and community development.

title: Two more Madison alders will vote to fire interim police monitor - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis. -- The alders for Madison's 14th and 15th Common Council Districts announced Thursday they would vote to fire the city's interim Independent Police Monitor. Alders Noah Lieberman and Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford's decisions mean nine alders have now publicly announced support to end Monitor Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass's appointment, including Dist. 2 Alder Will Ochowicz who introduced the resolution. Lieberman said the vote was "by far the most challenging decision I have had to make as alder" but said Glass needs to go to make sure the Office of the Independent Monitor remains effective. He said he still supports the Monitor's Office and its mission and still wants accountability for Madison police. "I will keep pushing for answers and policy changes from MPD to address the severe racial disparities in use of force and arrest rates," Lieberman said. "But I no longer believe that keeping IM Glass in her role is an effective way to get those answers or changes." He said his vote was not impacted by Glass' presence at protests following the police killing of Corey Ruiz, or her altercation with police in August that led to Green Bay police recommending charges against her to the Dane County District Attorney. In the aftermath of the altercation, Glass said she would "burn this city down." "While I would hope that I wouldn't use the IM's language following an encounter like that, I know that we can't be fully in control of our words in that sort of situation," Lieberman wrote. "I am disappointed in how the IM has responded to criticism of those words, but I don't think the actions of that day should impact our vote on this matter." Instead, Lieberman pointed to more administrative issues involving Glass, the biggest being her failure to bring in her permanent replacement. Glass was hired as an interim, and her job description included a stipulation that she would not be eligible for the permanent role. However, Lieberman said members of the Police Civilian Oversight Board have floated the idea of directly appointing Glass as the permanent monitor and Glass has done little to dissuade that idea. "I do not have faith that IM Glass would effectively pursue the recruitment and appointment of someone else to the role of permanent IM if she were to continue to serve in the interim role," he said. "Seeing as this is one of the two primary roles of the interim IM position, I cannot vote to allow her to continue in this role." Lieberman pointed to a review of Glass by City Attorney Michael Haas that identified multiple instances where Glass did not follow city policy, including hiring outside counsel and investigators without a city-approved contract. He also raised concerns with Glass's conduct towards some Common Council members, saying that she described some alders as "evil." He said Glass' office has been poor in its communication and hasn't clearly given updates to the public on work being done. Lieberman also criticized the eroding relationship between Glass and Madison Police Chief John Patterson. "While the cause of this rift is in dispute, the OIM cannot effectively implement reforms without a working relationship with the police chief," he said. "It does not appear to me that this will be the case so long as IM Glass is running the office. Martinez-Rutherford raised similar concerns, saying Glass is an affable person who "has exhibited behavior that gives me pause and causes me to question her judgment as a leader who is employed by the city." She said Glass's refusal to follow city rules sets a "disturbing precedent." "We must have police oversight and we must have an office that is committed to collaborating and actually doing that work," Martinez-Rutherford said. "I want to ensure that the PCOB and the OIPM are focused on the work of oversight and not encumbered by distractions that prevent the success of the work." Lieberman and Martinez-Rutherford's announcements put Glass' employment further into jeopardy. With nine alders publicly in support of her firing, only two more will need to vote for the resolution in order for it to pass. title: Madison's southside welcomes new full-service grocery store - Channel 3000
text: After years of planning, setbacks and construction, Maurer’s Urban Market opened its doors on Oct. 10 with a ribbon-cutting celebration led by Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. But why all of the fanfare? This city-owned grocery store is on Madison’s southside, an area that’s faced concerns of becoming a food desert, with the only other full-service grocery store, a Pick ‘N Save at 1312 Park St., plagued with closing rumors for the past decade. Plans for a new grocery store on the southside date back to 2017, when Milwaukee-based Rule Enterprises and Madison nonprofit Movin’ Out built an apartment building with room for a grocer on the ground level. The owner of Luna’s Groceries , a food retailer in Madison’s Allied-Dunn’s Marsh Neighborhood, was slated to fill the space, but pulled out of the project in 2021. That same year, the city purchased the commercial space for $4.6 million to revive the project, and in 2024, Kristie Maurer signed a 15-year lease with the city. Maurer first moved to Madison in 2010 to help her father open Fresh Madison Market on University Avenue. Since then, Kristie has helped manage grocery stores throughout Wisconsin, but this Park Street project felt different to her. “Had it been just about being a grocery store owner, I could have done that a long time ago. For me, it was about this project in Madison, in urban retail, in an arena that I think is really important, showcasing what can be done in a designated food desert space,” Maurer says. Maurer didn’t want to just create any grocery store; she wanted to create a retail space that would provide the southside community with the same quality food and facilities available in other areas of town — especially since food deserts most often affect those without reliable transportation, like the elderly population and low-income households. Along with the usual offerings, like produce, meat, seafood and grab-and-go meals, the 24,000-square-foot store is selling local goods, like kringles from Lane's Bakery and tamales from farmers’ market favorite, Tortillas Los Angeles. The grocer will also offer high-tech shopping carts that show customers a running total as they add items to it. These will be available soon. Since the market’s opening over the weekend, Maurer has been pleased by the community response. “I'm so pleasantly surprised by the amount of family and the amount of neighbors that have said, ‘We've been waiting for you. Thank you for being here.'” Even more, she’s excited about what the future holds for the rest of Madison’s southside. “There's a lot of development happening in Madison in general, but I think in south Madison, specifically, is an area where a lot of things are happening for continued growth and improvement,” Maurer says. “I'm super excited that the grocery store is now open so that we can be a key player in that.” Lily Spanbauer is associate editor at Madison Magazine. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY MADISON MAGAZINE. Students will take to the polls to decide Wisconsin’s governor, control of the State Legislature and various local races. Here is information and endorsements for key races for students organized as it will be presented on your ballot. Governor/Lt. Governor: David Crowley/Sarah Godlewski (D) vs Tom Tiffany/David Varnam (R) The Wisconsin gubernatorial election is contested between the Democratic ticket of David Crowley and Sarah Godlewski and Republicans Tom Tiffany and David Varnam. Incumbent Democrat Tony Evers decided not to seek reelection. The governor of Wisconsin is the most powerful office in the state, wielding a powerful veto pen over legislation, and appoints members to many of Wisconsin’s agency boards, like the Department of Natural Resources. David Crowley emerged from a chaotic primary, while running mate Godlewski faced no challengers in hers. Tiffany faced little opposition in his primary, and Varnam beat his opponent. Crowley has served as the Milwaukee County executive since 2020, previously serving two terms in the state assembly. Tiffany has served in Congress as the representative of Wisconsin’s 7th district since 2020 as part of the far-right House Freedom Caucus. Endorsement: We endorse David Crowley. His work as Milwaukee County Executive shows his ability to follow through on his promises, demonstrated through his work on affordable housing, public health and public safety in Milwaukee. We support Crowley’s pledge to raise the minimum wage, protect labor agreements and repeal Act 10 — Tiffany has voted and pledged to vote for policies that hurt the working class, like voting to weaken protection for victims of sexual harassment in the workplace, according to the Milwaukee Courier. We are concerned by Tiffany’s stance on abortion — he supports bans at the state and federal lebel, even cosponsoring a 2023 bill in Congress to ban abortions nationwide after six weeks of pregnancy without exceptions for rape or incest, according to WPR . Crowley has pledged to protect abortion rights. Crowley’s policies outline expanding state housing programs and investing in affordable housing, while Tiffany supports relaxing housing regulations, which could harm students looking for affordable housing and renter’s protection. Crowley said he would protect existing LGBTQ+ rights, including access to gender-affirming care while Tiffany opposed gender-affirming medical treatment for minors and said public funding should not cover it, including for adults. With the U.S. already at a “fragile democracy” standing, we cannot afford to elect the election-denier Tom Tiffany. Tiffany was the only Wisconsin representative to support the lawsuit challenging Biden’s legitimate victory in the 2020 election, according to Wisconsin Watch. Attorney General: Josh Kaul (D) vs Eric Toney (R) The Wisconsin Attorney General election is contested between incumbent Democrat Josh Kaul and Republican Eric Toney. The Attorney General oversees the Wisconsin Department of Justice, responsible for investigating and prosecuting major crimes. Kaul is seeking a third term, having first been elected in 2018 and winning reelection in 2022. Toney was the district attorney for Fond du Lac county from 2012 to 2024. Endorsement: We endorse Josh Kaul for Attorney General. Josh Kaul has repeatedly challenged the legislature in Wisconsin and the Federal government in an attempt to restore funding for infrastructure and public schools. Kaul is a consistent advocate for mental health programs and continues to fight against initiatives attempting to dismiss mental health regimes. In July 2025, Kaul joined a lawsuit against the Department of Education in retaliation for their budget cuts on mental health programs for K-12 schools. He stated that students need mental health funding in order to succeed in class. We align with Kaul’s viewpoint on mental health programs and its importance in education and the well-being of students. Secretary of State: JoCasta Zamarripa (D) vs Jay Schroeder (R) The Wisconsin Secretary of State election is contested between Democrat JoCasta Zamarripa and Republican Jay Schroeder, with incumbent Sarah Godlewski having won the Democratic primary for Lieutenant Governor. The office has also had its powers drawn down, accelerated by former governor Scott Walker’s feud with Doug La Follette. The Secretary of State now primarily serves as the clerk of the government, keeping laws and records. Zamarripa currently serves on the Milwaukee Common Council, having previously served 10 years in the state assembly for District 8 in Milwaukee. Schroeder has advanced to a single election in four attempts, losing the Secretary of State election to La Follette in 2018 by 155 thousand votes. Endorsement: We endorse JoCasta Zamarripa. Zampirra’s 10 years of experience in the State Assembly prove dedication to Wisconsin and its residents and we believe this experience will inform her advocacy for cost-of-living and worker’s rights and support her efforts toward modernizing the record-keeping office. We support Zamarripa’s commitment to maintaining the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission — Schroeder is campaigning on moving the role of Chief Election Official back to the Secretary of State, according to Ballotpedia . Zamarripa said that while the Secretary of State position is partisan, she will be honored to serve every Wisconsinite, regardless of party affiliation, according to the EagleHerald . Conversely, Schroeder describes himself as an “authentic MAGA activist,” according to the Wisconsin Examiner . State Treasurer: Yee Leng Xiong (D) vs John Leiber (R) The Wisconsin State Treasurer election is contested between Democrat Yee Leng Xiong and incumbent Republican John Leiber. The State Treasurer has had its powers drawn down by the legislature since 1995, and mostly oversees the banking of the state. Xiong has served on the D.C. Everest Area school board since 2014 and has worked as the director of a nonprofit organization. Leiber is seeking a second term, winning election in 2022. Endorsement: We endorse Yee Leng Xiong for State Treasurer. Xiong has made transparency in the management of public funds a centerpiece of his campaign, and he has spoken directly to the challenge of helping Wisconsin families build long-term economic security. His platform centers on expanding low-interest Trust Fund Loans for school construction and essential infrastructure. We share his commitment to Wisconsin families and to the schools they depend on. Representative in Congress District 2 (Uncontested): Mark Pocan (D) The Wisconsin Second Congressional District is uncontested, with incumbent Democrat Mark Pocan set to return to Congress for his eighth term. Pocan first won the seat in 2012, succeeding at the time Senator Elect Tammy Baldwin. Representative to The Assembly All State Assembly districts in student populated areas are expected to be won by the Democratic candidates. No State Senate elections are taking place around UW. This is the first full cycle of the State Senate under the new maps that were approved in 2024. Democrats are aiming to take both chambers after falling short of a majority in either in 2024. Your ballot will vary based on your neighborhood. Districts with high student populations are listed below. State Assembly District 76: Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford (D) vs Nina Chat (R) District 76 is contested between Democrat Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford and Republican Nina Chat for Francesca Hong’s seat, who lost a close primary to David Crowley in the Governor’s race. The district sits on the eastern portion of the isthmus, running from Capitol Square up to the airport and MATC downtown campus. Martinez-Rutherford is currently the Alderwoman for District 15 of the Madison Common Council and would be the first transgender state legislator in Wisconsin. Chat does not appear to have a campaign page or much public information available. Endorsement: We endorse Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford. Martinez-Rutherford has robust progressive policy solutions to increase affordability, expand healthcare and housing access, protect LGBTQ rights and abortion access, and fund public schools. We believe her experience as an Alder and her background in the service industry will prepare her to bring a fresh perspective to the State Assembly and help her to execute her clear plan for Wisconsin’s future. State Assembly District 77: Renuka Mayadev (D) vs Jane McCormick (R) District 77 is contested between incumbent Democrat Renuka Mayadev and Republican Jane McCormick. The district includes the entirety of the UW campus, Shorewood Hills village and encompasses the Regent, Monroe, Greenbush and Vilas neighborhoods off campus. Mayadev won the seat in 2024 after emerging from a crowded primary field. McCormick is a real estate broker who has not previously held office. Endorsement: We endorse Renuka Mayadev. We align with Mayadev’s vision for protecting reproductive freedom, strengthening public schools, supporting climate justice and improving access to healthcare. Mayadev’s commitment to advocacy and her work in the Assembly makes us confident that she will continue to support the district that includes our campus. State Assembly District 78: Sheila Stubbs (D) vs Henry Johnson (R) District 78 is contested between incumbent Democrat Sheila Stubbs and Republican Henry Johnson. The district starts south of Haywood Drive, extending to the southwestern edge of Madison, including all of Monona. Stubbs has served in the Assembly since 2019, moving districts in 2024 after the previous district maps were thrown out by the Wisconsin Supreme Court. Johnson is a college student at UW, according to The Isthmus . Endorsement: We endorse Sheila Stubbs. We believe in Stubbs’ goals of supporting criminal justice reform, increasing access to healthcare and protecting Wisconsin’s environment. Stubbs’ record in the Assembly proves she knows how to work across party lines to create effective legislation, and we are confident in her ability to continue to make progress for the Madison area. Dane County Sheriff (Uncontested): Kalvin Barrett (D) The Dane County Sheriff election is uncontested, with incumbent Democrat Kalvin Barrett set to retain the office. The County Sheriff is responsible for overseeing the county sheriff department. Barrett was first elected in 2022, having previously served as an officer in the Sun Prairie police department and the Dane County Sheriff’s Office. Dane County Clerk of the Circuit Court (Uncontested): Jeff Okazaki (D) The Dane County Clerk of the Circuit Court election is uncontested, with incumbent Democrat Jeff Okazaki poised to take the office. The Clerk of the Circuit Court handles the records of the court and manages the jury selection system. Okazaki was appointed to the position by Governor Tony Evers in 2023 before being elected to the post by voters in 2024. Referendums: Besides the previously stated candidates, there will be three Republican-led state constitutional amendments on your ballot this November. Wisconsin is one of 24 states that do not have initiative and referendum, according to Ballotpedia . This means Wisconsin is a state that doesn’t allow citizens to place constitutional amendments on the ballot through a direct initiative or petition process. Now what do these referendums really mean? The following interpretations of these referendums came from Wisconsin Watch . Question 1: Partial veto. Shall section 10 (1) (c) of article V of the constitution be amended to prohibit the governor, in exercising his or her partial veto authority, from creating or increasing or authorizing the creation or increase of any tax or fee? We encourage voters to vote no because the amendment is aimed at diminishing the powers of the Governor’s veto pen on a partisan basis. Evers used the veto pen to edit the state budget in 2023 to increase funding for public schools for 400 years. Republicans sued over the use of the pen, and the case found its way to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, which ruled in Evers favor. Reform to the veto pen should be on a bipartisan basis, not on sour partisan grapes. Question 2: Freedom to gather in places of worship during an emergency. Shall section 18 of Article I of the Constitution, which deals with religious liberty, be amended to prohibit the state or a political subdivision of the state from ordering the closure of, or forbidding gatherings in, places of worship in response to a state of emergency, including a public health emergency? We encourage voters to vote no because the constitutional amendment would weaken public healthcare policy in the future referring to emergencies like Covid-19. Question 3: Governmental entity discrimination prohibited. Shall section 27 of Article I of the Constitution be created to prohibit governmental entities in the state from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration? We encourage voters to vote no because the amendment would limit opportunities for disadvantaged groups and intends to weaken the individual rights and liberties of Americans regardless of Civil Rights laws. We believe the language of the question is intentionally trying to confuse the voters and it is actually targeting DEI related efforts.
